source.title_on_document: Large Language Models show both individual and collective creativity comparable to humans

supplement.where: Supplementary Materials, PDF pp. 30-84 (Supplementary Text, Tables S1 to S22, Figs. S1 to S8); tasks and data at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.24878421 (p. 19, p. 29)
supplement.holds: Table S4 (pp. 39-42): per-task means, SDs, ns, 95% CIs of the difference, t, df, P, and Cohen's d for each LLM versus humans; Table S5 (pp. 44-47): within-response cosine similarity and Levenshtein distance with t-tests; Table S6 (pp. 48-49): between-response similarity averaged across all pairs, no tests; Tables S11-S13: top-10 shares and collective-creativity results

paper_design_summary: 467 applicants to a Master's programme in China completed 13 creative tasks (divergent thinking, scientific and social problem solving, creative writing) without AI as part of an admission exam; five LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude, Qwen, SparkDesk) answered the same tasks repeatedly. Five trained raters scored all responses blind to source, and the paper places each LLM in the human percentile distribution, compares within- and between-response text similarity, and measures how many humans one LLM asked 10 times equals in contributing top-10 responses. No participant used AI.

studies.label: LLM versus human responses on 13 creative tasks (individual and collective creativity)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Human participants were randomly assigned to one of two test forms (Form A or Form B, each holding a different subset of the tasks). AI was not assigned; no participant used AI.
assignment.quote: The participants were randomly assigned to Test A (n = 237) or B (n = 230) and completed the tasks in the order specified above.
assignment.locator: p. 21, Materials and Methods, Human data collection
assignment.prereg_locator: Full document reviewed, including Materials and Methods (PDF pp. 19-24) and supplementary materials (pp. 30-84); no preregistration statement or identifier is reported.

participants.exclusions: Per-task human n varies (for example 230 on Divergent Thinking Task 1, 418 on Creative Advert Writing in Table S4) because each person took one of two forms and raters screened out invalid responses (Table S1).
participants.who: Applicants sitting a computer-based admission assessment for a social-science Master's programme; 330 female, 137 male; age 21 to 53 (mean 27.56); all with a Bachelor's degree; 103 current students and 140 current employees. Comparison corpus: responses from GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude, Qwen, and SparkDesk (about 50 rated responses per LLM per task).
participants.quote: A total of 467 human participants from China (330 female, 137 male; age ranging from 21 to 53 years, with a mean of 27.56 and SD of 6.03
participants.locator: p. 6, Results; p. 21, Human data collection

ai_tool.how_used: The LLMs produced their own responses to the same Chinese-language tasks (GPT models via API at temperatures 0 to 1; Claude, Qwen, SparkDesk via web portals at default settings), with added instructions to be original. Humans did not use AI. (p. 22)

task.description: 13 creative tasks in three domains: two scenario-based divergent thinking tasks (ideas to keep warm or pick fruit on a desert island), three scientific and three social problem-solving tasks (PISA 2022 style), and five creative writing tasks (advert for an elder-care robot, keyword-prompted stories, emoji-prompted stories and continuation).
task.duration: 5 to 7 minutes per task; keyword-prompted writing 10 + 10 minutes (pp. 19-20)

outcomes.name: Percentile rank of each LLM in the human distribution, averaged across all indicators of the 13 tasks
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Five trained raters (psychology students) per round, Consensual Assessment Technique, ratings generally on a 1-5 scale, except Social Problem Solving Task 1 flexibility, which counts distinct categories among the three ideas on a 0-3 scale (pp. 19 and 23); ratings equated across two rating rounds by z-score linear equating. Indicators include creativity mean and max for divergent thinking (novelty x usefulness), originality or flexibility for problem solving, creativity and judge-rated diversity for writing. n_units counts the human participants; LLM responses number about 50 per LLM per task. The Discussion (p. 17) gives GPT-3.5 as 38th percentile, against 37th on p. 8.

contrasts.reported: five LLMs ranked on average in the 46th percentile; Claude and GPT-4 52nd, SparkDesk 44th, Qwen 42nd, GPT-3.5 37th; domain averages 55th (divergent thinking), 59th (problem solving), 25th (creative writing)
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Benchmarking LLMs against humans; p. 9, Fig. 2

outcomes.name: Collective creativity: size of human group that matches one LLM asked 10 times in contributing top-10 responses
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Rated responses pooled; group size N at which humans and 10 LLM responses contribute 50% each of the top-10 responses, 1000 bootstrap draws per N, averaged over five groups of 10 LLM responses and across tasks. Pooling all responses, LLMs contributed about 33% of the top-10 responses (p. 13, Table S11).

contrasts.treatment_arm: Individual LLMs asked 10 times; separately, pooled models in the Mixed LLMs analysis
contrasts.reported: For each individual LLM asked 10 times, equivalent human group size: GPT-4 10.42, Claude 9.99, SparkDesk 8.66, Qwen 8.64, GPT-3.5 7.71 (Fig. 6). Separately, the Mixed LLMs analysis pools all models and samples 10 to 50 responses in increments of five; y = 0.52x + 3.41, where x is pooled LLM responses and y is equivalent human group size, so roughly two additional pooled-model responses (1/0.52) equal one extra human (Fig. 7). The slope is not an individual-model estimate.
contrasts.locator: p. 15, Fig. 6; p. 16, Fig. 7; p. 14, text (Table S12)

outcomes.name: Rated creativity, Creative Advert Writing Task
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Overall creativity rating (novelty and usefulness), mean of five raters, 1-5 scale. Table S4 reports the same statistics for every task and LLM; results are mixed across tasks (for example GPT-4 above humans on keyword-prompted writing creativity, d = 1.416, p. 41).

outcomes.name: Between-response text similarity (cosine similarity of embeddings), Keyword-prompted Writing
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity of text-embedding-ada-002 embeddings, averaged across all pairs of responses within a source; Levenshtein distance also reported. Humans had the lowest between-response similarity on every task in Table S6.

contrasts.reported: Keyword-prompted Writing: LLMs n = 402, n (pairs) = 80601, cosine similarity 0.907, Levenshtein distance 0.897; Human n = 399, n (pairs) = 79401, cosine similarity 0.870, Levenshtein distance 0.922 (higher similarity means lower diversity, so LLM diversity is lower). No test reported.
contrasts.locator: p. 49, Table S6; p. 12, Diversity within and between responses

diversity_detail.metric: Mean pairwise cosine similarity; mean pairwise Levenshtein distance
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of responses within a source (each LLM, all LLMs pooled, or all humans) for each task
diversity_detail.uncertainty: None reported; Table S6 gives averages only
diversity_detail.notes: Sign: the paper reports similarity; higher similarity means less diversity. Pooled-LLM pair count 80601 plus human 79401 gives n_units 160002.

outcomes.name: Judge-rated diversity between one source's two stories, Keyword-prompted Writing
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Raters scored how different each participant's (or LLM response's) two stories are from each other, 1-5 scale. Within-response embedding similarity (Table S5, pp. 44-47) points the same way on most tasks.

outcomes.name: Fluency: valid ideas per response across the two divergent-thinking tasks
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Counts of valid ideas in a complete response, summarized across the two divergent-thinking tasks in the Results. The paper does not print the exact denominator, SD or test for this aggregate mean, so n_units is null. Task-specific raw response and idea counts appear in Table S1 (p. 32).

contrasts.reported: Humans generated an average of 3.68 valid ideas; LLMs generated a mean of 8.85 valid ideas per response, ranging from 5.43 for SparkDesk to 12.47 for GPT-4. Descriptive means only; no inferential comparison is reported here.

outcomes.name: Idea novelty, Divergent Thinking Task 1
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Novelty is the extent to which an idea is uncommon and unique; each valid idea is rated separately, using the source-blind rating procedure and 1-5 scale (pp. 19 and 23). These are idea-level statistics, with multiple ideas per response; n_units = 748 + 856 = 1604 valid ideas, not people. Serial-position comparisons are variants of these ratings (Table S3 and Figs. S4-S8).

contrasts.locator: PDF p. 35, Table S2, Divergent Thinking Task 1, Novelty

outcomes.name: Idea usefulness, Divergent Thinking Task 1
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Usefulness is how practical and effective an idea is at addressing the problem; each valid idea is rated separately, using the source-blind rating procedure and 1-5 scale (pp. 19 and 23). These are idea-level statistics; n_units = 748 + 856 = 1604 valid ideas, not people. Serial-position comparisons are variants of these ratings (Table S3 and Figs. S4-S8).

contrasts.locator: PDF p. 35, Table S2, Divergent Thinking Task 1, Usefulness

outcomes.name: Creativity mean and maximum within a response, Divergent Thinking Task 1
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Each idea receives a creativity proxy equal to novelty multiplied by usefulness (p. 10). Mean and maximum summarize the same rated ideas within a response and are retained together as alternative summaries. Table S4 compares complete responses: n_units = 50 + 230 = 280 responses for either summary, not the count of individual ideas. Temperature and prompt variants are reported in Tables S7-S8 and S16.

contrasts.reported: Mean creativity: GPT-4 M = 4.725 (SD 0.309, n = 50 responses) vs Human M = 4.770 (SD 1.320, n = 230 responses); 95% CI of the difference [-0.236, 0.147]; t = -0.456; df = 276.777; P = 0.649; Cohen's d = -0.037. Maximum creativity: GPT-4 M = 7.336 (SD 1.082, n = 50 responses) vs Human M = 6.494 (SD 1.913, n = 230 responses); 95% CI of the difference [0.450, 1.235]; t = 4.248; df = 125.693; P < 0.001; Cohen's d = 0.470.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 10, Divergent thinking; p. 39, Table S4, Divergent Thinking Task 1, Creativity Mean and Creativity Max

outcomes.name: Originality of bicycle improvements, Scientific Problem Solving Task 1
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: The methods define this as originality, although Table S4 labels the row Creativity. The three proposed bicycle improvements are rated separately and their average indicates the response originality (p. 19); ratings use the procedure on p. 23. n_units = 51 + 237 = 288 complete responses, not individual ideas.

contrasts.reported: GPT-4 M = 2.497 (SD 0.301, n = 51 responses) vs Human M = 1.948 (SD 0.374, n = 237 responses); 95% CI of the difference [0.440, 0.660]; t = 9.836; df = 286; P < 0.001; Cohen's d = 1.518.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 19, Scientific Problem Solving tasks; p. 40, Table S4, Scientific Problem Solving Task 1

outcomes.name: Flexibility of water-saving ideas, Social Problem Solving Task 1
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Judges score the number of distinct categories among a response's three water-saving ideas, using a 0-3 scale (pp. 19 and 23). The final rating is averaged across judges. n_units = 51 + 229 = 280 complete responses; the ideas within a response are not independent observations.

contrasts.reported: GPT-4 M = 2.843 (SD 0.367, n = 51 responses) vs Human M = 2.306 (SD 0.58, n = 229 responses); 95% CI of the difference [0.410, 0.665]; t = 8.381; df = 113.21; P < 0.001; Cohen's d = 0.982.
contrasts.locator: PDF pp. 19 and 23, task scoring and Rating procedure; Table S4, p. 40 (n, M, SD, CI, t, df, P) and p. 41 (Cohen's d), Social Problem Solving Task 1

outcomes.name: Rated creativity, Keyword-prompted Writing
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Overall creativity rating under the procedure on pp. 20 and 23. Originality, imagination, surprisingness, interpretation of keywords and connection of keywords were also rated; the paper uses the overall rating in its analysis. Table S4 reports response-level n: 50 model responses and 221 human responses (n_units = 271); Table S1 separately reports 399 valid human stories. The methods do not explicitly state the aggregation rule for creativity across the valid stories within a response.

contrasts.reported: GPT-4 M = 3.341 (SD 0.51, n = 50 responses) vs Human M = 2.417 (SD 0.681, n = 221 responses); 95% CI of the difference [0.755, 1.094]; t = 10.825; df = 93.123; P < 0.001; Cohen's d = 1.416.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 20, Keyword-prompted Creative Writing; p. 33, Table S1; p. 41, Table S4, Keyword-prompted Writing, Creativity

outcomes.name: Judge-rated difference between two stories, Emoji-prompted Writing Task 1
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Judges rate how different the two stories from the same participant or model response are (pp. 20 and 23), on a 1-5 scale. This is within-response variety, coded as flexibility. n_units = 50 + 201 = 251 two-story responses; this is the judge-rated denominator in Table S4, not the different denominator for computed similarity in Table S5.

contrasts.reported: GPT-4 M = 2.743 (SD 0.67, n = 50 responses) vs Human M = 3.082 (SD 0.725, n = 201 responses); 95% CI of the difference [-0.561, -0.116]; t = -3.002; df = 249; P = 0.003; Cohen's d = -0.474.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 20, Emoji-prompted Creative Writing; p. 42, Table S4, Emoji-prompted Writing Task 1, Diversity

outcomes.name: Rated creativity, Emoji-prompted Writing Task 2
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Overall creativity of one story connecting the supplied emojis, rated under the procedure on pp. 20 and 23. Originality, imagination, surprisingness, interpretation of emojis and connection of emojis were also rated; the paper uses the overall rating. n_units = 50 + 181 = 231 stories. Temperature-specific analyses are reported in Tables S7-S8.

contrasts.reported: GPT-4 M = 1.476 (SD 0.258, n = 50 stories) vs Human M = 2.602 (SD 0.777, n = 181 stories); 95% CI of the difference [-1.261, -0.992]; t = -16.497; df = 222.21; P < 0.001; Cohen's d = -1.612.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 20, Emoji-prompted Creative Writing; p. 42, Table S4, Emoji-prompted Writing Task 2, Creativity

outcomes.name: Within-response text similarity between two stories, Keyword-prompted Writing
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity from text-embedding-ada-002 embeddings compares the two stories within each response (pp. 11-12 and 24); Levenshtein distance is a second measure of the same within-response variety. One observation is a complete two-story response, so n_units = 50 + 178 = 228. Independent-sample t-tests compare the response-level similarity scores (Table S5); these are not all pairs across different people. Higher cosine similarity means less variety, so direction is coded treatment_lower while the printed positive similarity effect is retained. Temperature variants appear in Tables S9-S10.

contrasts.reported: Cosine similarity: GPT-4 M = 0.928 (SD 0.016, n = 50 responses) vs Human M = 0.883 (SD 0.026, n = 178 responses); 95% CI of the difference [0.038, 0.051]; t = 14.639; df = 125.280; P < 0.001; Cohen's d = 1.829. Levenshtein distance: GPT-4 M = 0.882 (SD 0.048, n = 50 responses) vs Human M = 0.921 (SD 0.023, n = 178 responses); 95% CI of the difference [-0.054, -0.026]; t = -5.670; df = 55.554; P < 0.001; Cohen's d = -1.310.
contrasts.locator: PDF pp. 11-12, Diversity within and between responses; p. 24, Statistical Analysis; p. 46, Table S5, Keyword-prompted Writing; p. 47, t-test note

eligibility.reason: No person received AI assistance: random assignment concerned Test A (237 people) or Test B (230 people), and LLM responses were collected separately (PDF pp. 21-22). The human sample contains 467 people, with task-specific valid-response exclusions; for example, 230 human responses are analyzed for Divergent Thinking Task 1 and 418 for Creative Advert Writing (Table S4, pp. 39 and 42). Creativity was rated on produced responses and similarity was computed from their text (PDF pp. 6 and 23-24). Criteria 2 and 3 are met, but criterion 1 is not; retain AI-versus-human context evidence.

one_line_finding: Across 13 creative tasks the five LLMs ranked on average in the 46th percentile of 467 human test-takers (Claude and GPT-4 52nd, creative writing 25th; p. 8, Fig. 2), LLM responses were more similar to each other than human responses on every task (Table S6, pp. 48-49), and one LLM asked 10 times matched 7.71 to 10.42 humans in contributing top-rated responses (p. 15, Fig. 6).
notes: Outcome coverage is capped at 15 entries under form-spec rule 7. The individual and collective benchmarks are listed first; original outcome IDs are preserved. Added entries cover fluency, idea novelty and usefulness, response-level mean/maximum creativity, scientific originality, social flexibility, keyword-writing creativity, emoji-writing creativity and within-response variety. The detailed task-specific contrasts use GPT-4 versus humans, consistent with the original examples; other model contrasts remain in Tables S2, S4 and S5. Not separately extracted: Divergent Thinking Task 2 novelty, usefulness and creativity mean/max; Scientific Problem Solving Tasks 2-3 and Social Problem Solving Tasks 2-3 originality (Table S4, pp. 39-41); Emoji-prompted Writing Task 3 creativity (Table S4, p. 42); within-response similarity for tasks other than keyword writing (Table S5, pp. 44-47); and task-specific between-response similarity beyond keyword writing (Table S6, pp. 48-49). Mean/max creativity and cosine/Levenshtein measures are grouped as alternative summaries within their outcome entries. Serial-position analyses (Table S3, Figs. S4-S8), temperature analyses (Tables S7-S10), prompt variants (Table S16), writing subscales (p. 20), and detailed collective-creativity task/domain results (Tables S11-S13) are not separate outcome entries. Human-only test-form balance and demographic analyses (Tables S14-S15 and S17-S22), including the Remote Association Task used for test-form balance, do not estimate AI-versus-human creativity or AI assistance.
